The balance of the fund marked MEX$9.5 billion (0.04 percent of GDP) by the end-2020 compared to MEX$158 billion (0.6 percent of GDP) in the previous year.","locator":"page 84","attribution":"IMF staff calculations; SHCP data","period_fit":"2019-2020; pertains to economic shock management relevant to 5B.9 and 5B.10 evaluation periods","source_limitations":["Fund balance data as of end-2020; end-2021 balance not shown in this excerpt","Does not isolate which revenue shortfalls were pandemic-induced versus structural"],"question_ids":["5B.9","5B.10"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0002","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"The Mexican authorities estimated that a FEIP balance of MEX$100 billion (approximately 0.35% of 2022 GDP) would constitute an adequate fiscal contingency for 2023, but the actual balance was MEX$25.0 billion (0.09% of 2022 GDP) as of end-June 2022.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"adverse","actor":"Mexican authorities; FEIP","action":"established fiscal contingency target; reported actual balance","mechanism":"budget stabilization fund balance measurement","outcome":"Actual FEIP balance (MEX$25.0B, 0.09% GDP) was 75% below the authorities' own adequacy threshold (MEX$100B, 0.35% GDP) for 2023","dates":["end-June 2022","2023 (target year)"],"quantities":["MEX$25.0 billion (0.09% of 2022 GDP) actual balance","MEX$100 billion (0.35% of 2022 GDP) adequacy threshold"],"excerpt":"the authorities estimate that a balance of around MEX$100 billion in FEIP (0.35 percent of 2022 GDP and 0.33 percent of 2023 GDP) would provide for an adequate fiscal contingency for 2023, the balance in the fund was MEX$25.0 billion (0.09 percent of 2022 GDP) as of end-June 2022","locator":"page 84","attribution":"Mexican authorities; SHCP","period_fit":"2022-2023; directly relevant to economic shock management capacity evaluation","source_limitations":["Balance as of end-June 2022; year-end position may differ","Threshold is the authorities' own estimate, not an independent benchmark"],"question_ids":["5B.9","5B.10"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0003","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexico's fiscal framework was respected in only 7 of the 13 years to 2020, with escape clauses invoked during 2010-12 and 2014-16, and the inflexibility of the framework is identified as a key factor in this record.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"adverse","actor":"Mexican fiscal framework (FBFRL)","action":"invoked escape clauses; failed to maintain balanced budget","mechanism":"escape clause triggers under the Balanced-Budget Rule and Public Sector Borrowing Requirement Rule","outcome":"Framework respected in 7 of 13 years (2008-2020); attributed to framework inflexibility","dates":["2008-2020 (13-year period)","escape clauses used 2010-12 and 2014-16"],"quantities":["7 of 13 years framework respected","13-year evaluation period"],"excerpt":"Escape clauses were used in 2010-12 and 2014-16, meaning that the framework was only respected in 7 out of the 13 years to 2020. The inflexibility of the current framework is deemed to be a key factor in this","locator":"page 87","attribution":"IMF staff assessment (IMF 2020 cited)","period_fit":"2008-2020; demonstrates chronic framework inadequacy relevant to 5B.3 and 5B.10","source_limitations":["IMF staff assessment rather than raw quantitative measurement","Cites IMF 2020; underlying trigger data not reproduced verbatim in this excerpt"],"question_ids":["5B.3","5B.10"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0004","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"IMF staff assessed that Mexico's proposed 2023 fiscal framework reforms represent a pragmatic step for immediate risks but increase complexity, do not improve reliability, and do not address the pro-cyclical bias of the existing framework.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"mixed","actor":"IMF staff","action":"assessed proposed 2023 fiscal framework reforms","mechanism":"qualitative policy evaluation against reform criteria","outcome":"Reforms rated as pragmatic but inadequate: complexity increases; reliability unchanged; pro-cyclical bias unaddressed","dates":["2023 (proposal year)"],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"The reforms represent a pragmatic step forward in enabling fiscal policy to respond to immediate downside risks, but comprehensive reform is necessary to improve flexibility and reliability while ensuring transparency and fiscal responsibility. But this approach also entails trade-offs, with complexity increasing as a result and knock-on consequences for transparency. Moreover, as the additional funding for FEIP is predicated on whatever headroom against the debt ceiling is left at year-end, the extent of financing is subject to uncertainty and therefore unreliable. Finally, the reforms do not address the pro-cyclical bias in the current fiscal framework","locator":"page 86","attribution":"IMF staff assessment","period_fit":"2023 reform proposals; relevant to evaluating whether fiscal rules protect macroeconomic stability (5B.3)","source_limitations":["IMF staff opinion rather than measured outcome","Proposal stage; effects not yet materialized"],"question_ids":["5B.3","5B.9"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0005","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Since 2019, income and corporate tax revenues and VAT revenues have grown as a share of GDP, with expected increases of 1.0 and 0.6 percentage points of GDP respectively between 2019 and 2022, attributed at least partially to tax administration reforms.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"favorable","actor":"Mexican tax administration; SAT (Servicio de Administración Tributaria)","action":"implemented tax compliance reforms; generated revenue increases","mechanism":"abolition of tax credit offsetting; digital platform withholding; GAAR; BEPS compliance; corporate merger prohibition","outcome":"Income/corporate tax: +1.0% of GDP; VAT: +0.6% of GDP (2019-2022 expected)","dates":["2019-2022"],"quantities":["1.0 percentage point of GDP increase in income/corporate tax","0.6 percentage point of GDP increase in VAT","MEX$170 billion reduction in VAT evasion (2018-2021)"],"excerpt":"Since 2019, income and corporate tax and VAT revenues have grown as a share of GDP, with expected increases of 1.0 and 0.6 percent of GDP between 2019 and 2022, respectively. This strong revenue performance is deemed to be at least partially due to the bedding-in of compliance policies","locator":"page 90","attribution":"IMF staff; Mexican tax authorities","period_fit":"2019-2022; relevant to evaluation of tax policy fairness (5B.8) and anti-corruption/rule enforcement (5B.5)","source_limitations":["Causal attribution is qualified ('at least partially'); isolating impact is acknowledged as difficult","Successive shocks complicate isolation of reform effects from other factors"],"question_ids":["5B.5","5B.8"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0006","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexico's authorities' own VAT gap analysis suggests a reduction in VAT evasion of approximately MEX$170 billion between 2018 and 2021.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"favorable","actor":"Mexican tax authorities (SAT)","action":"conducted VAT gap analysis","mechanism":"tax gap measurement comparing theoretical to actual VAT collections","outcome":"Estimated MEX$170 billion reduction in VAT evasion, 2018-2021","dates":["2018-2021"],"quantities":["MEX$170 billion reduction in VAT evasion (2018-2021)"],"excerpt":"the authorities' new focus on non-compliance at the border may also represent a tougher challenge given the overlap with security issues and the need for close coordination between the tax administration and the army, which has taken over the physical customs inspection functions","locator":"page 90","attribution":"Mexican authorities (VAT gap analysis)","period_fit":"2018-2021; relevant to tax compliance enforcement evaluation","source_limitations":["VAT gap methodology and assumptions not specified in this excerpt","Self-reported by authorities; IMF does not independently verify the VAT gap estimate in this passage"],"question_ids":["5B.5","5B.8"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0007","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexico implemented comparatively less macroeconomic policy stimulus in 2020-21 than other countries during the COVID-19 pandemic, resulting in a smaller unemployment gap as a source of inflationary pressures.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"context","actor":"Government of Mexico","action":"implemented macroeconomic stimulus","mechanism":"fiscal stimulus magnitude relative to peer countries","outcome":"Less stimulus than comparator countries; smaller unemployment-driven inflationary pressure","dates":["2020-2021"],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"MEXICO comparatively less macroeconomic policy stimulus in 2020–21. The unemployment gap as a source of inflationary pressures has thus been less of a concern than elsewhere.","locator":"page 81","attribution":"IMF staff assessment","period_fit":"2020-2021 pandemic period; relevant to shock management evaluation (5B.9) and economic trajectory assessment (5B.10)","source_limitations":["Comparative statement without quantitative benchmark (e.g., stimulus as % of GDP vs. comparator countries)","No specification of which countries serve as comparators"],"question_ids":["5B.9","5B.10"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0008","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Empirical analysis using a hybrid Philips curve approach confirms that rising energy and food prices were the primary drivers of the 2021-22 headline inflation surge in Mexico, with these factors explaining much of the surge through 2021Q3, after which residual cost-push factors also contributed.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"context","actor":"IMF staff","action":"conducted empirical Philips curve analysis","mechanism":"hybrid Philips curve estimation (2003-2019 sample period, 2021-22 dynamic forecast)","outcome":"Energy and food price shocks confirmed as primary drivers of 2021-22 inflation surge; residual cost-push factors also contributed upward pressure especially in 2022Q1","dates":["2021Q1-2022Q2 (analysis period)","2003-2019 (estimation sample)"],"quantities":["Hybrid Philips curve estimated on 2003-2019 data applied to 2021Q1-2022Q2 dynamic forecast","Equal weights on expected (0.52) and lagged (0.48) inflation for headline"],"excerpt":"Empirical analysis confirms that rising energy and food prices resulted in the increase in headline inflation. A Philips curve approach to analyze the inflation surge in 2021-22 suggests that the factors identified above explain much of the surge in headline inflation through the third quarter of 2021, notably rising energy and then food prices. While these factors continue to explain much of the above-target inflation subsequently, residual cost push factors also contributed upward inflationary pressures, especially in the first quarter of 2022.","locator":"page 81","attribution":"IMF staff calculations","period_fit":"2021-2022; directly relevant to inflation management and shock response evaluation (5B.9)","source_limitations":["Philips curve estimation omits the pandemic period due to 'exceptional volatility'","Results deemed 'broadly robust' but not definitively validated against alternative specifications in this excerpt"],"question_ids":["5B.9"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0009","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"The hybrid Philips curve estimates for Mexico show approximately equal weights on expected inflation (0.52) and lagged inflation (0.48) for headline inflation, consistent with the conventional view that past inflation surprises have a relatively greater and longer-lasting role in emerging market economies compared to advanced economies.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"context","actor":"IMF staff","action":"estimated hybrid Philips curve coefficients","mechanism":"reduced-form regression of headline and core inflation on expectations, lagged inflation, unemployment gap, and relative price shocks","outcome":"Expected inflation weight: 0.52; Lagged inflation weight: 0.48; Supports longer inflation persistence in Mexico vs. advanced economies","dates":["2003Q1-2019Q4 (estimation sample)","2021Q1-2022Q2 (forecast application)"],"quantities":["0.52 weight on expected (survey-based, 12-month-ahead) inflation","0.48 weight on lagged (past) inflation","R² = 0.75 for headline inflation equation"],"excerpt":"The estimated Philips curve suggests that both expected and lagged inflation contribute to current headline inflation. The results presented in the table suggest roughly equal weights in the case of headline inflation (0.52 versus. 0.48). This result is broadly in line with the conventional view of a relatively greater role of past inflation in contributing to current inflation dynamics in Mexico and other emerging market economies compared to advanced economies.","locator":"page 81","attribution":"IMF staff calculations","period_fit":"2003-2022; estimation sample 2003-2019; forecast period 2021-2022; relevant to monetary policy credibility evaluation (5B.3)","source_limitations":["Estimation omits pandemic period (2020) due to exceptional volatility","Survey-based inflation expectations may themselves be biased","Conclusions described as 'broadly robust' to different specifications, not definitively validated"],"question_ids":["5B.3","5B.9"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0010","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Between 2010 and 2017, Mexico hedged 210-215 million barrels of oil exports annually through put options, with strike prices set by a technical committee at SHCP generally consistent with the assumed oil price in the government budget.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"context","actor":"Government of Mexico; SHCP (Ministry of Finance) technical committee","action":"conducted annual oil hedging through put options","mechanism":"put options on oil exports; technical committee sets volume and strike price","outcome":"210-215 million barrels hedged annually 2010-2017; strike prices aligned with budget assumptions; hedging operations are a primary FEIP financing source","dates":["2010-2017"],"quantities":["210-215 million barrels hedged annually (2010-2017)"],"excerpt":"Strike prices are generally consistent with the assumed oil price in the budget and 210–215 million barrels were hedged in this way between 2010 and 2017.","locator":"page 84","attribution":"SHCP; IMF staff","period_fit":"2010-2017; relevant to fiscal rule credibility and macroeconomic stability evaluation (5B.3)","source_limitations":["Hedging program not directly linked to Mexico's economic cycle; does not function as automatic fiscal stabilizer","No information on hedging outcomes (costs, benefits, whether options were exercised)","Data period ends 2017; more recent hedging activity not shown"],"question_ids":["5B.3"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0011","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"The Structural Current Spending Rule (SCR) covers only 36% of total public expenditures, excluding interest payments, fuel for electricity generation, CFE and PEMEX expenditures, and Federal government investment, leaving substantial spending outside the rule's constraint.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"adverse","actor":"Mexican fiscal framework (FBFRL Structural Current Spending Rule)","action":"established expenditure rule with limited coverage","mechanism":"structural spending rule with explicit exclusions","outcome":"Only 36% of public expenditures covered by the spending rule; large segments (PEMEX, CFE, interest, investment) excluded","dates":[],"quantities":["36% of total public expenditures covered by SCR","Exclusions: interest payments, fuel for electricity generation, CFE expenditures, PEMEX expenditures, Federal government investment"],"excerpt":"It accounts for 36 percent of total public expenditures. Under Article 18 of the FBFRL any proposed increase of expenditures in the budget beyond the permitted growth must be accompanied by a revenue or spending cut initiative to neutralize its effect.","locator":"page 87","attribution":"FBFRL (Federal Budget and Fiscal Responsibility Law); IMF staff","period_fit":"Current framework as of 2022-2023; relevant to evaluation of fiscal rule credibility (5B.3)","source_limitations":["36% coverage figure is from current framework description; historical evolution not shown","Does not assess whether exclusions are policy-justified or constitute loophole-riddling"],"question_ids":["5B.3"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0012","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"The Balanced-Budget Rule (BBR) in Mexico is broadly procyclical, contributing to fiscal policy that amplifies rather than dampens economic cycles, and Mexico's fiscal framework was only respected in 7 of 13 years to 2020.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"adverse","actor":"Mexican fiscal framework (Balanced-Budget Rule)","action":"applied balanced budget requirement","mechanism":"cash-basis balanced budget rule covering Federal government, PEMEX, CFE, IMSS, ISSSTE, and trust funds","outcome":"Framework described as broadly procyclical; respected only 7 of 13 years (2008-2020)","dates":["2008-2020"],"quantities":["7 of 13 years framework respected"],"excerpt":"The Balanced-Budget Rule (BBR) requires that the budget must be balanced on a cash basis, excluding investments by PEMEX and its subsidiaries. The coverage of this rule includes the Federal government, PEMEX and CFE, and IMSS and ISTE, and various trust funds. The rule is broadly procyclical.","locator":"page 87","attribution":"IMF staff assessment","period_fit":"2008-2020; relevant to evaluation of fiscal rule credibility and macroeconomic stability (5B.3) and economic trajectory (5B.10)","source_limitations":["'Broadly procyclical' is an IMF staff characterization","The 7-of-13 years statistic is repeated from the escape clause discussion; underlying year-by-year data not in this excerpt"],"question_ids":["5B.3","5B.10"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0013","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexico's Fondo Mexicano de Petróleo (FMP) sovereign wealth fund held reserves of approximately USD 1 billion (0.07% of GDP) as of July 2022, far below the 3% of GDP threshold that would expedite approval of transfers from FMP reserves to FEIP, rendering such transfers practically unavailable.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"adverse","actor":"Fondo Mexicano de Petróleo (FMP)","action":"accumulated and maintained sovereign wealth reserves","mechanism":"oil revenue collection and transfer; statutory reserve accumulation rules","outcome":"Reserves at 0.07% GDP (~$1 billion) vs. 3% GDP threshold for expedited transfer; reserves too low to serve as contingency backstop","dates":["July 2022"],"quantities":["USD 1 billion (0.07% of GDP in 2022) FMP Long-Term Reserves","3% of GDP threshold for expedited FMP-to-FEIP transfer"],"excerpt":"Since 2018, reserves have been roughly equal to USD 1 billion (0.07 percent of GDP in 2022). FMP reserves can be used directly for budgetary needs even when they are below 3 percent of GDP but FEIP resources must be completely exhausted first and a two-thirds majority vote by the Chamber of Deputies is required.","locator":"page 83","attribution":"FMP; IMF staff","period_fit":"2022; relevant to fiscal contingency capacity evaluation (5B.9) and economic trajectory (5B.10)","source_limitations":["Reserve level as of July 2022 only; trajectory not shown","Threshold mechanism described but whether two-thirds majority was ever attempted not discussed"],"question_ids":["5B.9","5B.10"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0014","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexico abolished the right to offset excess tax credits against other taxes, required digital platforms to withhold taxes on intermediary transactions, implemented General Anti-Abuse Rules (GAAR), prohibited company mergers for tax purposes, and enacted OECD BEPS Actions 2, 4, and 12 — all since 2019.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"favorable","actor":"Mexican government; SAT","action":"enacted multiple tax administration reforms","mechanism":"legislative and administrative reforms targeting tax compliance, corporate planning, and cross-border transactions","outcome":"Comprehensive tax administration reform package; each reform listed separately","dates":["2019 onward"],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"The abolition of the right to offset excess tax credits against other taxes, building on staff recommendations regarding tackling large-scale tax fraud; The requirement that digital platforms withhold taxes due on transactions in which they acted as intermediary; Implementation of General Anti-Abuse Rules (GAAR) and the prohibition of company mergers for tax purposes to tackle corporate tax planning; And enaction of actions 2, 4 and 12 in the OECD's Base Erosion and Profit Shifting (BEPS) agenda.","locator":"page 90","attribution":"Mexican government; OECD BEPS framework","period_fit":"2019 onward; relevant to anti-corruption/rule enforcement (5B.5) and tax fairness (5B.8)","source_limitations":["Reform passage does not assess implementation quality or enforcement outcomes","Does not quantify revenue impact of individual reforms vs. the package as a whole"],"question_ids":["5B.5","5B.8"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[],"premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0015","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"IMF staff estimated that ratification of the proposed 2023 fiscal framework reforms before end-2022 could free up MEX$20-30 billion for FEIP, but characterized this financing as uncertain because it depends on year-end headroom against the debt ceiling.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"mixed","actor":"IMF staff","action":"estimated fiscal reform impact on FEIP financing","mechanism":"proposed debt-issuance IOU mechanism for FEIP replenishment","outcome":"MEX$20-30 billion potential FEIP increase; characterized as uncertain dependent on debt ceiling headroom","dates":["2023 (proposal year)"],"quantities":["MEX$20-30 billion estimated FEIP increase under proposed reforms"],"excerpt":"The ratification of the proposed reforms before the end of 2022 are expected to free up MEX$20–30 billion for FEIP. Moreover, as the additional funding for FEIP is predicated on whatever headroom against the debt ceiling is left at year-end, the extent of financing is subject to uncertainty and therefore unreliable.","locator":"page 86","attribution":"IMF staff assessment","period_fit":"2022-2023 proposal; relevant to fiscal contingency capacity (5B.9)","source_limitations":["Staff estimate, not confirmed outcome","'Expected' financing is contingent on year-end conditions not known at time of assessment","Proposal not yet ratified at time of document"],"question_ids":["5B.9"],"verification_status":"pending","verification_notes":[],"premium_verification_required":false}],"inspected_locator_count":10,"locator_dispositions":[{"locator":"page 81","disposition":"evidence_extracted","explanation":"Contains IMF empirical analysis on inflation drivers (energy/food prices), Philips curve estimates with specific coefficients (expected inflation 0.52, lagged 0.48), comparative stimulus assessment, and inflation persistence findings relevant to 5B.3 and 5B.9."},{"locator":"page 82","disposition":"evidence_extracted","explanation":"Contains regression table with Philips curve coefficient estimates for headline and core inflation, including raw food price coefficients (0.20 headline, 0.02 core), unemployment gap coefficients, REER, and R² values (0.75/0.77 headline, 0.33/0.34 core). Relevant to 5B.3 and 5B.9."},{"locator":"page 83","disposition":"evidence_extracted","explanation":"Describes FMP sovereign wealth fund mechanics and reserves (USD 1 billion, 0.07% GDP as of 2022), FMP transfer amounts (MEX$673B in 2022 vs. MEX$364B in 2021), statutory reserve rules, and the 3% GDP threshold for expedited FMP-to-FEIP transfers. Relevant to 5B.3 and 5B.9."},{"locator":"page 84","disposition":"evidence_extracted","explanation":"Contains FEIP balance data (MEX$158B end-2019 to MEX$9.5B end-2020), FEIP transfer to budget (MEX$157B, 0.7% GDP), oil hedging operations (MEX$47B in 2020), 210-215 million barrels hedged annually 2010-2017, authorities' MEX$100B adequacy threshold vs. MEX$25B actual balance, and characterization of FEIP replenishment prospects. Relevant to 5B.3, 5B.9, and 5B.10."},{"locator":"page 85","disposition":"evidence_extracted","explanation":"Describes proposed 2023 fiscal framework reforms creating new FEIP financing mechanism via debt-issuance IOUs, enabling FEIP to hold financial assets, and assessment that reforms mitigate immediate spending concerns while reducing oil-price dependency. Relevant to 5B.3 and 5B.9."},{"locator":"page 86","disposition":"evidence_extracted","explanation":"Contains IMF staff critical assessment of proposed reforms: pragmatic for immediate risks but increases complexity, does not improve reliability, does not address pro-cyclical bias, and financing is uncertain and predicated on debt ceiling headroom. Also contains MEX$20-30B staff estimate. Relevant to 5B.3 and 5B.9."},{"locator":"page 87","disposition":"evidence_extracted","explanation":"Contains detailed fiscal framework design features table including SCR (36% coverage), BBR (procyclical), PSBR, escape clauses (5 specified triggers), and 7-of-13-years compliance record. Key design features table is material evidence for 5B.3 and 5B.10 evaluation."},{"locator":"page 88","disposition":"no_material_evidence","explanation":"FSAP (Financial Sector Assessment Program) recommendations table is focused on financial sector oversight, cybersecurity, macroprudential policy, and crisis management — not directly relevant to any 5B question on fiscal policy, economic management, tax administration, or macroeconomic stability."},{"locator":"page 89","disposition":"no_material_evidence","explanation":"Continuation of FSAP recommendations table covering financial development issues (fintech, climate finance). No material evidence relevant to 5B.1-5B.10 questions on economic management quality."},{"locator":"page 90","disposition":"evidence_extracted","explanation":"Contains detailed tax administration reforms (abolition of tax credit offsetting, digital platform withholding, GAAR, corporate merger prohibition, BEPS Actions 2/4/12) and quantified revenue outcomes (income/corporate tax +1.0% GDP, VAT +0.6% GDP, VAT evasion reduced MEX$170B 2018-2021). Relevant to 5B.5 and 5B.8."}],"material_omissions":["Pages 88-89 (FSAP recommendations) omitted no material economic management evidence for 5B questions — FSAP is financial sector stability focused, not fiscal/economic management quality focused.","The document covers only pages 81-90 of a larger IMF Country Report; full context of Mexico's economic trajectory, actual budget execution data, and PEMEX financial状况 not available in this excerpt.","IMF staff recommended comprehensive reforms (debt anchor, tightened definitions, expanded expenditure rules, medium-term sustainability strategies) but these are not yet enacted — evidence of what was actually done, not what was recommended, is being evaluated."],"unresolved_gaps":[{"question_ids":["5B.1","5B.2","5B.4","5B.6","5B.7","5B.8"],"gap":"No evidence in pages 81-90 addresses whether the ruler appointed qualified economic professionals through credible processes and empowered their operational independence (5B.2), whether competition and entrepreneurship laws were created and enforced (5B.4), whether enacted budgets produced quality infrastructure/education/health outcomes (5B.6), whether the ruler published reliable economic information and corrected failed programs (5B.7), or how tax/labor/wage/regional policies distributed gains across classes and regions (5B.8 beyond tax administration). Pages 81-90 are IMF technical analysis of inflation dynamics, fiscal framework design, and tax administration reforms — not evidence about these specific governance quality questions."},{"question_ids":["5B.10"],"gap":"Pages 81-90 do not contain a comprehensive assessment of whether the ruler left a stronger and more durable economic trajectory than inherited, accounting for implementation lags, external conditions, institutional constraints, and distribution. The documents describe fiscal framework flaws and contingencies, but do not make an overall trajectory judgment for 5B.10."}]}
